Orlando di Lasso. A Franco-Flemish composer of extraordinary prolific genius who lived from 1532 to 1594 and was celebrated equally for madrigals, motets, and chansons across all major European courts. His mastery of both text-painting and structural perfection made him arguably the most admired composer of the late Renaissance.

Lasso composed over two thousand works across all sacred and secular genres, including over one thousand motets alone. This staggering output was maintained across six decades. He was a master of the madrigal, crafting vivid dramatic settings with sophisticated text-painting. His madrigals range from intimate love lyrics to violent narratives like La dolce vista. He served as maestro di cappella at the court of Duke Albrecht of Bavaria in Munich for thirty-eight years, the most stable and prestigious post of his era.

His motets show remarkable stylistic adaptability. Some embrace the strict Counter-Reformation piety associated with Palestrina, while others employ more emotionally expressive Baroque gestures. He excelled in the secular chanson tradition, composing witty French texts with driving rhythms and sophisticated rhyme schemes. What unified his vast output was masterful counterpoint, harmonic sophistication, and an uncanny ability to match musical language to poetic content. He worked across languages including Latin, Italian, French, and German, each with different rhythmic and sonorous demands, and he met each one perfectly.
